summary.text: At \(n=9\), direct calculation gives \(a(9)=49{,}770{,}428{,}644{,}836{,}901=29^2\cdot59{,}180{,}057{,}841{,}661\), so this term is not squarefree. Thus the universal squarefreeness claim—and therefore the conjunction—fails, irrespective of the infinitude claim.

full_proof.text:
Let the primes in increasing order, indexed from zero, be
\[
p_0=2,\quad p_1=3,\quad p_2=5,\quad \ldots,
\]
and define the primorial
\[
P_n=\prod_{k=0}^{n-1}p_k.
\]
Thus the sequence in question is
\[
a(n)=P_n^2+1.
\]
(The product is empty when \(n=0\), giving \(a(0)=2\), in agreement with the stated indexing.)

We disprove the assertion that every term is squarefree by considering \(n=9\). The first nine primes are
\[
2,3,5,7,11,13,17,19,23.
\]
For completeness, these are indeed precisely the primes up to \(23\): their primality follows by trial division by primes no larger than their square roots, and every other integer from \(2\) through \(23\) is visibly composite. Explicitly, the omitted integers are
\[
4,6,8,9,10,12,14,15,16,18,20,21,22,
\]
with respective evident factors among \(2,3,5,7,11\). Therefore
\[
P_9=2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot7\cdot11\cdot13\cdot17\cdot19\cdot23.
\]
Computing this product in stages gives
\[
2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot7=210,
\]
\[
11\cdot13=143,\qquad 17\cdot19=323,
\]
and hence
\[
210\cdot143=30030,
\]
\[
30030\cdot323=9{,}699{,}690,
\]
\[
P_9=9{,}699{,}690\cdot23=223{,}092{,}870.
\]

Now consider the square of the prime \(29\). We have \(29^2=841\), and
\[
223{,}092{,}870=841\cdot265{,}271-41.
\]
Indeed,
\[
841\cdot265{,}271
=(800+40+1)\cdot265{,}271
=212{,}216{,}800+10{,}610{,}840+265{,}271
=223{,}092{,}911.
\]
Thus
\[
P_9\equiv -41\pmod{841}.
\]
Squaring and adding one yields
\[
P_9^2+1\equiv (-41)^2+1=1681+1=1682=2\cdot841\equiv0\pmod{841}.
\]
Consequently,
\[
29^2=841\mid P_9^2+1=a(9).
\]

The same calculation may be written as an exact factorization. Since \(P_9=841m-41\) with \(m=265{,}271\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
a(9)
  &=(841m-41)^2+1\\
  &=841^2m^2-82\cdot841m+1682\\
  &=841\bigl(841m^2-82m+2\bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]
Substitution of \(m=265{,}271\) gives
\[
a(9)=841\cdot59{,}180{,}057{,}841{,}661
     =49{,}770{,}428{,}644{,}836{,}901.
\]
This is exactly the sequence term obtained directly from
\[
223{,}092{,}870^2+1=49{,}770{,}428{,}644{,}836{,}901.
\]

It remains only to connect this divisibility to squarefreeness. An integer is squarefree precisely when no square of a prime divides it (equivalently, no square \(d^2\) with \(d>1\) divides it). The integer \(29\) is prime: it has no divisor among \(2,3,5\), the only primes not exceeding \(\sqrt{29}\). Since
\[
29^2\mid a(9),
\]
the term \(a(9)\) is not squarefree.

Therefore the universal claim
\[
\forall n,\quad a(n)\text{ is squarefree}
\]
is false. The conjecture under consideration is the conjunction of this universal squarefreeness claim with the assertion that \(a(n)\) is prime for infinitely many \(n\). A conjunction is false as soon as either conjunct is false. Hence the explicit counterexample at \(n=9\) disproves the combined conjecture, independently of whether infinitely many prime terms exist.
